These are words you use to talk about earthquakes.
first aid kit
a package containing medical supplies
(noun)
Example: Emily said that earthquake experts advise  people to have a first aid kit on hand that includes bandages, scissors, and tweezers.
engenn10le14ob02aud02
bandage
cloth used to cover and protect injuries
(noun)
Example: You should wrap a bandage around the injury.
engenn10le14ob02aud03
tweezers
small metal device used to hold or pull something
(noun)
Example: Earthquake experts advise people to have tweezers inside the first aid kit.
engenn10le14ob02aud04
structure
something ​built, such as a ​building or a ​bridge
(noun)
Example: Luckily, she was far away from any bridge or similar structure.
engenn10le14ob02aud10
tremor
a slight earthquake
(noun)
Example: She has also learned to hide under sturdy furniture when she feels the slightest tremor.
engenn10le14ob02aud06
to take cover
to protect oneself by ducking down into or under a shelter
(expression)
Example: She remembers standing against an inner wall, but she could have taken cover under a piece of furniture for better protection.
engenn10le14ob02aud07
aftershock
a sudden movement of the Earth's crust after an earthquake, which is less violent in nature
(noun)
Example: She also could have known more about the aftershocks.
engenn10le14ob02aud08
to collapse
to  fall down suddenly
(verb)
Example: Since those aftershocks, she has been afraid to drive on bridges, overpasses and ramps because she saw a bridge collapse in an aftershock crushing a few cars.

strong or solid
(adjective)
Example: Because she has experienced an earthquake, she has also learned to hide under sturdy furniture when she feels the slightest tremor.

Present Perfect and Past Tenses
You can combine the Present Perfect tense with the Past Tense.
You combine the Present Perfect tense with the Past Tense to:
1. To describe events that have continued since a specific time in the past.

For example:
The dog has moved.
2. To describe repeated feelings towards a past event.

For example:
Ever since I saw Star Wars, I have wondered if George Lucas would make another trilogy.
You can also use the Present Perfect twice in the same sentence.

For example:
Since I've lived in Toronto, I've always gone to the Kensington Market.
Look at some examples from the text:
Ever since my teacher, Emily, relayed her earthquake experience in Kobe to me, I've had an acute fear of earthquakes!
She has become an expert in earthquake safety since she witnessed that massive earthquake in 1995.
She has also learned to hide under sturdy furniture when she feels the slightest tremor.
I moved to California three months ago, and since then my fear of earthquakes has transformed into full-blown anxiety.
Speculating about Past Events: Could Have
You can use could have to speculate about past events. Specifically, you use it to speculate about scenarios different from what actually occurred.
You can use could have in the following situation:
1. To express past possibility

For example:
He could have been a doctor if he had applied himself in school.
1. To express past uncertainty

For example:
I'm not really sure who called. It could have been Candice, I guess.
You can use could have in the negative form.

For example:
He couldn't have been a doctor.
It couldn't have been Candice.
Couldn't have can also be used with a comparative adjective:

For example:
We chose the red version, and we couldn't have been happier.

images.text:
In Japan there have been many earthquakes since the dawn of time. A teacher that I had was there in 1995 when a massive earthquake struck early in the morning.
Ever since my teacher, Emily, relayed her earthquake experience in Kobe to me, I've had an acute fear of earthquakes! Emily told me that she couldn't have survived a very destructive earthquake by good fortune alone. People she knew in Japan had given her advice. Still, she could have been better prepared. She has become an expert in earthquake safety since she witnessed that massive earthquake in 1995.

Emily said that earthquake experts advise  people to have a first aid kit on hand that includes bandages, scissors, and tweezers.  She has also learned to hide under sturdy furniture when she feels the slightest tremor. She remembers standing against an inner wall, but she could have taken cover under a piece of furniture for better protection. She said the quake was so violent that her huge television inside a heavy cabinet was jumping around that morning.

She also could have known more about the aftershocks. She said those were absolutely terrifying. Since those aftershocks, she has been afraid to drive on bridges, overpasses and ramps because she saw a bridge collapse in an aftershock crushing a few cars. Emily now realizes she could have died because of the aftershocks. Luckily she was far away from any bridge or similar structure. She said that the aftershocks may be felt up to several months after the earthquake. Another thing to know is that damaged buildings should be avoided, and authorities will tell you when it is safe to enter a building again.
I moved to California three months ago, and since then my fear of earthquakes has transformed into full-blown anxiety. Still, I am glad Emily has given me safety tips and advice which I have kept in the forefront of my brain, just in case.
